reading.rtitle: The Objection Is Not the Problem
paras: Salespeople are trained to answer objections, and that training may be the reason so many deals stall. An objection is a reason the other side gives for not agreeing yet, and the first one is almost never the real one. Price is the classic example: when somebody says the price is too high, they might mean the price is too high, but more often they mean that they cannot defend it internally, which is a completely different problem and has a completely different answer.

The pattern that works is unglamorous and it has three moves. First, acknowledge what was said, in their words, without softening it. Second, reframe: find the concern underneath and say it out loud, which is the part almost nobody does. Third, redirect to something that can actually be tested. A supplier who says you may want to look at the liability clause before we talk about price is not avoiding the objection. They are answering the one that matters, and they are doing it with a modal verb that leaves the buyer room to disagree.

The language does more work here than the argument. This will solve it and this might solve it are the same claim at two different temperatures, and the second one survives being wrong. Experienced negotiators use the weakest form that still says the thing, because pushback is not a failure of persuasion, it is information arriving. The ones who hold their ground on everything win the meeting and lose the account. The ones who meet halfway on everything have no leverage left by the second round. The useful skill is knowing which of the two you are doing, and being able to say so in one sentence.

items: I hear you on the price, and I think the real question is the timeline.

listenings.text: Early on I used to treat an objection like an exam question. Somebody says the price is too high and I would have three answers ready, and I would deliver all three, and the deal would die anyway. What I do now is much slower. I repeat what they said, in their words, and then I say the thing I think is actually going on, and I say it as a question. Something like, it sounds like the number is not the issue, it is that you would have to defend it to somebody who was not in this meeting. About half the time they say yes, that is exactly it, and then we are having a completely different conversation, which is the one that was going to decide it anyway. The other half they correct me, and that is just as useful, because now I know.

The thing I had to unlearn was the word must. In my language it is soft. You say it to a colleague and it sounds like a suggestion. I would sit in a meeting in English and say you must consider the audit risk, and I could see the temperature in the room change, and I had no idea why, because in my head I had said something perfectly friendly. A very kind counterpart told me eventually. He said, when you say must, it sounds like my boss talking. Try might. So now I say you might want to look at that before Thursday, and the strange thing is that people actually do it. The weaker word gets the stronger result, and it took me about four years to believe that.
